articles.title: Observing Comet Tempel 1
articles.summary: Jane and Mojo recount their experience observing Comet Tempel 1 from Mount Wilson on the night of the Deep Impact mission, sharing views with a CUREA program audience using their portable telescopes. Despite the comet's faintness and atmospheric conditions, they managed to glimpse it and confirmed its brightening, thrilled to be part of the worldwide observation effort. The article also includes a detailed calendar of August and September activities for the San Jose Astronomical Association.

articles.title: New Discounts for Club Members
articles.summary: This article announces new discount programs available to club members. Oceanside Photo and Telescope (OPT) now offers up to a 10% discount on merchandise, requiring a specific code at checkout. Additionally, Sam Sweiss of Scope City in San Francisco continues to provide discounts, which can be more substantial on high-margin items, emphasizing local customer service.

articles.title: Beyond The Terminator
articles.summary: The article "Beyond The Terminator" recounts the author's personal journey and evolving perspective on lunar observing, initially sparked by a memorable night of Earthshine viewing and encounters with fellow astronomers. Despite the prevalent "Aperture Fever" for deep-sky objects, the author's enthusiasm led him to start a column for the Ephemeris on lunar and planetary observing, which went through several name changes including "The Shallow Sky," "Lunacy," and ultimately "Mooning." This narrative reflects on the shift in astronomical observing attitudes and the author's enduring, albeit self-professed non-expert, fascination with the Moon.

articles.title: Is Mars as Large as the Moon? You Bet!
articles.summary: This article debunks a widespread internet hoax claiming Mars will appear as large as the Moon to the naked eye in August, tracing the misinformation back to a garbled email misinterpreting a 2003 close opposition. The author clarifies that Mars, though brightening, will not be unusually large and advises readers to be skeptical of unverified internet claims. It also briefly mentions other observable celestial events for August 2005, such as Mercury and Venus.

articles.title: AstroCon 2005
articles.summary: AstroCon 2005, the AANC Conference and Workshops, is scheduled for August 27th, 2005, at the Randall Museum in San Francisco, hosted by the San Francisco Sidewalk Astronomers. The event, themed "Celebrating Bay Area Astronomy" and honoring John Dobson's 90th birthday, features notable speakers, workshops, a star party, and award presentations for a $25 registration fee. The article also provides a guide to celestial observations for August, including planets like Neptune and Uranus, and details about the Perseid Meteor Shower.

articles.title: Marian Chuang – August 20
articles.summary: Marian Chuang, a systems engineer specialist for Lockheed Martin, will be the speaker at the August 20 general meeting. Her presentation will focus on her current project: advanced planning for human missions to the Moon and Mars, specifically addressing bioastronautics, which covers the physiological and psychological aspects of long-duration space flight. Chuang previously worked on projects such as Gravity Probe-B and the Spitzer Space Telescope.

articles.title: Music of the Spheres Program at Lick
articles.summary: Lick Observatory is hosting its "Music of the Spheres" summer concert series to benefit its Visitors Program. The event features live music, talks by research astronomers, and telescope viewing (weather permitting), with various ticket options available. Tickets can be purchased through the UCSC Ticket Office, and more information, including performers, is available on the UCO Lick website.

articles.title: Finding the Planet Mercury in Daylight Skies
articles.summary: Ernie Piini successfully observed and photographed the planet Mercury in daylight during its conjunction with Venus on June 27, 2005. Despite visual challenges, he used an 8-inch Newtonian telescope and a Canon "Rebel" digital camera, first locating the Sun with a solar filter, then using setting circles to find Venus. Although he couldn't visually discern Mercury, image enhancement software confirmed its presence in his photographs alongside Venus, marking a personal achievement.

articles.title: SJAA loaner scope status
articles.summary: This document outlines the status of the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) loaner scope program, detailing which telescopes are currently available for immediate loan, those recently loaned out, and those with extended loan periods. SJAA members can contact Mike Koop to borrow a scope, with instructions on how to pick up available scopes and how a waiting list is managed for others.
